Example 6.1 — HIV-1 Protease Inhibitors with PDB Structures: Overlay of the Four Most Potent¶

A reproducible record of an AI-assisted BindingDB analysis: each prompt, the BindingDB tool calls that answered it with their recorded results, the answer, and its figures. Run all cells to show the recorded results, or rerun every call on your own copy of the database and check each result against the recorded one.

  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Model: claude-opus-5-5
  • Data: BindingDB release 202611 (BDB-mySQL_All_202611_dmp.zip, SHA-256 daea9260d404919a183ce02d91bf4b9c49b410bea7eaaeba105c8e0280510381)
  • Database build: 2026-11-21T01:08:15+00:00, DuckDB 1.5.6
  • Derived data: standard InChIKeys computed from SMILES by RDKit 2026.03.6; compound_property computed from SMILES (largest fragment) by RDKit 2026.03.6
  • Server: mcp-bindingdb v0.1.17, commit 79dae5d22c0f
  • Software: python 3.12.7, duckdb 1.5.6, rdkit 2026.03.6, mcp 2.3.0, gemmi 0.7.5
  • Notebook generated: 2026-11-24T04:55:57Z
  • Contents: 1 exchange · 5 tool calls · 1 figure

How to run¶

Keep the notebook in its folder, which holds everything it needs: requirements.txt (mcp-bindingdb at its commit and the versions of the packages it needs), the recorded results in data/, the figures in figures/ and the 3D viewers of the binding-site overlays in overlays/. With uv, from that folder (replace the path with yours):

cd /path/to/6.1-hiv1-protease-inhibitor-overlay-notebook
uv run --no-project --with-requirements requirements.txt --with jupyterlab jupyter lab 6.1-hiv1-protease-inhibitor-overlay-notebook.ipynb

then choose Run → Run All Cells. The first start installs the packages, which takes a minute or two; the cells show the recorded results, so no database is needed. Without uv: pip install -r requirements.txt jupyterlab, then jupyter lab 6.1-hiv1-protease-inhibitor-overlay-notebook.ipynb in the folder.

How to rerun the calls¶

To rerun every BindingDB call on your own copy of release 202611 and check each result against the recorded one, set RERUN = True in the setup cell and run all cells, or rerun the notebook without opening Jupyter, writing a copy with the new results:

cd /path/to/6.1-hiv1-protease-inhibitor-overlay-notebook
BINDINGDB_RERUN=1 uv run --no-project --with-requirements requirements.txt --with nbconvert jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --output 6.1-hiv1-protease-inhibitor-overlay-notebook-rerun.ipynb 6.1-hiv1-protease-inhibitor-overlay-notebook.ipynb

A rerun needs the database: the one BINDINGDB_DUCKDB=/path/to/bindingdb_202611.duckdb names (put it before uv run), else the newest one mcp-bindingdb built on this computer, for example for Claude Desktop. With neither, the first rerun builds one, which takes about half an hour and 2.4 GB. To build exactly release 202611, with a clone of mcp-bindingdb:

git clone https://github.com/sbl-sdsc/mcp-bindingdb.git
cd mcp-bindingdb
git checkout 79dae5d22c0f15b8ded9b49adc8b105f0463703a
scripts/build_duckdb.sh --release 202611

The setup cell checks the database's release and source checksum against the recorded ones.

Run as it is, each call cell shows its recorded result, read from data/ and checked against the SHA-256 digest recorded in the cell. Rerun, it shows the new result with ✅ when it matches the recorded one (floats to 10 significant digits, ids of viewers and files left out). Calls to PubChem, RCSB or PDBe depend on those services and may differ. The prose answers are the model's and are not recomputed.

In [ ]:
# Shows the results recorded during the session (data/), so the notebook runs without a database. Set
# RERUN = True (or start Jupyter with BINDINGDB_RERUN=1) to rerun every BindingDB call on a local copy of
# the database instead and check it against its recorded result: see 'How to rerun the calls' above.
from mcp_bindingdb.notebook import Replay

RERUN = False
replay = Replay(release='202611', source_zip_sha256='daea9260d404919a183ce02d91bf4b9c49b410bea7eaaeba105c8e0280510381', rerun=RERUN)

🧠 Assistant

The overlay just opened in your browser.

HIV-1 protease inhibitors with PDB structures. BindingDB splits the protease across many target records (different constructs and strains), so the answer depends on which record you look at. The richest is the Q7K/L33I/L63I/C67A/C95A construct (complex 125), which has 13 compounds with crystal structures of that protein, all with Ki values. The top of the list:

Compound Ki (nM) PDB entries
Nelfinavir (Viracept) 0.01 2PYM, 2PYN, 2Q63, 2Q64, 2QAK
TMC-126 0.0145 2I4U, 7LDY, 7M9Z
Darunavir 0.015 18 entries incl. 2IEN, 3BVB, 4HLA, 7MAP
Ritonavir 0.02 1RL8, 1SH9, 3NDW, 3NDX
GRL-0255A 0.026 3DJK
Cyclic compound 14c 0.0285 3I6O (same connectivity; stereochemistry not confirmed)
Amprenavir 0.04 16 entries incl. 1HPV, 3NU3, 3NU4
Saquinavir 0.04 3NDU, 3PWR, 3UFN
Indinavir (Crixivan) 0.07 1HSG, 1SDT–1SDV, 1SGU, 2B7Z
GRL-02031 0.099 3H5B, 3VF5, 3VF7, 3VFB, 4J55

A change in this BindingDB release (202611): of these, BindingDB itself now links only TMC-126 and amprenavir to their PDB entries. Nelfinavir, darunavir, ritonavir, saquinavir, indinavir and the GRL compounds were found by matching their InChIKeys against the ligands of the PDB's HIV-1 protease entries, so the list is the same as before, but it now rests on that match.

Other records add more: the A-series symmetric inhibitors A-76928 (Ki 0.011 nM, 1HVK) and A-77003 (0.012 nM, 1HVI/1HVS) and A-74704 (4.5 nM, 9HVP) on complex 50, which also has lopinavir (6PJB, with only an IC50 of 35 nM there); and the cyclic urea DMP323 (Ki 0.27 nM, 3JVW) on complex 56. Those come from different protease records, so their values aren't strictly comparable to the table above.

The overlay shows the four most potent from the consistent record — nelfinavir, TMC-126, darunavir and ritonavir — superposed on 3NDX (ritonavir, 1.03 Å, the best resolution of the four). The fits are tight: pocket RMSDs of 0.34–0.39 Å with no binding-site residue displaced more than 2 Å, so all four bind an essentially identical pocket conformation. What differs is the hydrogen bonding:

  • All four hydrogen-bond to the catalytic aspartates D25:A and D25:B — the transition-state hydroxyl engaging the catalytic dyad, the shared anchor of every peptidomimetic in this class.
  • Darunavir and TMC-126 are the most extensively hydrogen-bonded, with identical partner lists: both add D29:B, D30:A, D30:B and G27:B. Those bis-THF contacts into the backbone of the S2 subsite are exactly the design feature that makes darunavir hold up against resistance mutations — it grips main-chain atoms that can't mutate away.
  • Ritonavir instead reaches up to G48:B in the flap, along with D29:B and G27:B — a flap contact the others don't make.
  • Nelfinavir is the sparsest, only D25:A/B plus D30:A, consistent with its smaller, less peptide-like scaffold.

The entries are not all the same construct: 2PYN (nelfinavir) and 2I4U (TMC-126) share 92% and 95% sequence identity with the record's sequence, 2IEN and 3NDX 100%, which the pocket fit absorbs without trouble.

One caveat worth flagging: several of these Ki values rest on a single measurement (nelfinavir's 0.01 nM, ritonavir's 0.02 nM), and darunavir and TMC-126 on two each; 0.01 nM is below what most protease assays can resolve. The ranking among the top four is within assay noise — treat them as "all sub-0.1 nM" rather than genuinely ordered.
